ADVISORY_BODY: The real catalyst this morning isn't ES/NQ — it's the long end of the Treasury curve. The 10-Year yield rose as much as 4bps to 5.33%, pushing past its 2007 peak to the highest level since 2002, with the 30-Year also at a 2002 high (Bloomberg/Yahoo Finance). This is a continuation, not a one-day spike: the 10-Year closed Wednesday at 5.28% (a 19-year high at the time, CNBC/FXStreet) after a session where stocks initially rallied on a cooler Core PCE print (3.0% YoY vs 3.3% est., headline 3.4% vs 3.7% est.) before the bond and oil markets "ambushed" the rally into the close — the Dow fell 443 points even as the Nasdaq eked out a +0.25% gain (FXStreet). The nuance worth getting right: Oct-28 FOMC hike odds actually FELL to 39% Wednesday, down sharply from 81% the Friday before, after NY Fed President Williams struck a "no need for urgency" tone — genuinely dovish for the next meeting. But the 10-Year kept climbing anyway, because persistent inflation, heavy government borrowing and AI-infrastructure capex demand for capital are structural forces a single dovish Fed comment doesn't fix (Bloomberg). Read together: the market isn't pricing an imminent October hike — it has simply shifted the expected year-end hike toward the December 9 meeting while the fiscal/capex supply-demand imbalance keeps grinding yields higher regardless of which meeting does it. Layer in a fresh inflationary impulse: oil is up roughly 2% (WTI +2.06% to ~$92.28, Brent +2.61% to ~$100.60) on Middle East tensions and Chinese refiner export suspensions (TheStreet) — arriving at an inconvenient moment for anyone hoping the rates story is cooling. On the growth side, this morning's data leaned resilient: initial jobless claims fell to 197,000, below forecasts; ADP private payrolls reportedly added +90K; and Challenger-tracked job cuts fell 18% month-over-month (-39% year-over-year) to 43,281 in September (TheStreet) — good for earnings, but also exactly the kind of strength that keeps a December hike in play. ISM Manufacturing PMI (10:00 AM ET) is the next direct read on whether growth momentum is adding fuel to that fire. Our own tape is more two-sided than the headline change suggests: /ES is at 7,732.00 (+16.50 vs prior close, +0.21%) but that print sits BELOW both the classic pivot (7,736.33) and Wednesday's value area low (7,751.00) after an overnight high (7,767.75) that already faded back; /NQ at 30,813.00 (+114.25, +0.37%) looks stronger but is sitting on an even bigger giveback — its overnight high spiked to 31,151.50, briefly clearing the Donchian-20 upper band (31,094.75) and even poking above the classic R2 level, before fading roughly 340 points back to essentially flat against Wednesday's VWAP. Neither index has confirmed a breakout; both gave back an overnight pop. VIX at 16.40 has barely moved and remains historically complacent — the equity vol market has not repriced for a 24-year high at the long end, which is itself the instability to watch. Gold is holding firm (+0.34% to $4,200.80 on our feed) despite the real-rate headwind, which says the bid is coming from the oil/Mideast risk premium and fiscal-debasement hunger, not rate-cut hope. On single names: Accenture's beat-and-raise (+20.70% on FMP's live quote, $221.33) is lifting the entire IT-services/consulting peer group in sympathy — Cognizant +11.12%, EPAM +10.56%, Globant +10.40%, Infosys and Wipro both +10.00%, Gartner +8.22% (FMP) — a sector-wide tell on enterprise demand, not an isolated beat. Corteva's reported -81% move is NOT a crash — it's the technical price adjustment from today's scheduled Vylor Inc. seed-business spin-off distribution (TipRanks/Business Record), and should not be read as a decliner in the normal sense. Moderna is extending lower, -3.20% in today's premarket (TheStreet) after opening down 6.27% Tuesday on Citi's downgrade to Sell (price target actually raised to $80) following the stock's 703% run and a legal setback (Forbes/24-7 Wall St./GuruFocus). Nike reports Q1 FY2027 AMC tonight (consensus EPS $0.44/-10% YoY on $11.35B revenue, stock near a 12-year low around $36.48, Street Hold-leaning at 8 buy/16 hold/6 sell, TipRanks) — a single-name event, not a macro mover, but worth watching given how thin the tape's cushion looks today. Bottom line: the green-ish futures print is NOT confirmation that the rates shock is contained — both ES and NQ are trading below or barely at their reference value areas after fading overnight pops, VIX hasn't moved, and the structural yield story (fiscal borrowing + AI capex) is bigger than any single FOMC meeting's odds.

Analysis
The headline this week has flipped twice in 48 hours: Wednesday's cooler Core PCE (3.0% YoY vs 3.3% est.) and NY Fed Williams striking a "no urgency" tone on October pulled Oct-28 FOMC hike odds down to 39% (from 81% the Friday before) — genuinely dovish for the next meeting. But the 10-Year Treasury yield kept climbing anyway, hitting 5.33% this morning, the highest since 2002, because the move is being driven by persistent inflation, heavy fiscal borrowing and AI-infrastructure capex demand for capital — structural forces a single dovish Fed comment doesn't fix. Markets are effectively saying: not October, but the hiking cycle itself (most likely via December) and the deficit/capex supply-demand imbalance are not going away.
Spec. Move
ISM Manufacturing PMI (10:00 AM ET) is the next direct read on whether growth momentum is adding fuel to the fiscal/capex side of this story. This morning's claims (197K, below forecast) and ADP (+90K) already lean resilient-growth, which is a double-edged signal: good for earnings, but also exactly the kind of strength that keeps the Fed's December decision live.
Trade Idea
No new duration exposure (TLT-type) until the 10-Year itself turns, not just until a single FOMC meeting's odds fall. Treat today's calm equity tape as unconfirmed on the rates risk, not as an all-clear.
